title: Station-based thermal scores supplied 82% of the fish-larva temperature slope off California in 2000-2020
abstract: We tested whether a marine community thermal-index slope used geographic or seasonal thermal information. We split 1978-1999 CalCOFI taxon scores into additive station, quarter and remaining parts. We then tested 2,583 matched fish-larva and water samples at 45 stations in 2000-2020. With salinity and survey controls, the full temperature slope was 0.1221 index C per water C. The station part supplied 82.2% of this slope, with a conditional 95% year-jackknife interval of 79.8-84.6%. The season part supplied 15.1% and the remaining part 2.7%. Slopes add exactly. The station share stayed near 80% without the 2014-2016 heatwave and with species-like labels only. Thus the explicit season component of fitted scores did not supply most of this marine thermal link. This is a partition of score information, not a causal partition of phenology and movement or a spatial-tracking fraction. Fixed training scores, survey selection, coarse seasons and 21 year clusters limit inference. Code, source hashes, aggregate estimates and a retrieval method are included; raw data and record-level tables stay external.

display.caption: The station part supplied most of the held-out temperature slope. Bars show conditional 95% year-cluster intervals. All four fits use the same salinity and survey controls.

citations.reason: We adapt its MIT profile and survey code and reuse its source snapshots. We partition the thermal score slope that it measured.
The Northeast Shelf marine contrast motivates this score-information test in California.
